what_its_for: Clozapine is used to treat severe schizophrenia, especially when other medicines have not worked well. It may also help reduce the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in people with schizophrenia or a related condition called schizoaffective disorder. It works by balancing certain natural chemicals in the brain to help reduce symptoms like hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there) and disorganized thinking.
how_to_take: Take clozapine exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with food or milk. Swallow the regular tablet whole with a full glass of water. If you have the orally disintegrating tablet (ODT), place it in your mouth and let it dissolve completely — do not chew or swallow it whole. For the oral suspension (liquid), shake the bottle well before each use and use the measuring device provided — never use a household spoon. Do NOT stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause serious problems.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a very low dose and slowly increase it over several weeks. This helps reduce side effects. A typical starting dose is 12.5 mg once or twice a day. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on how you respond — most people end up on 300 to 450 mg per day, split into smaller doses. Some people may need up to 900 mg per day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, as your dose is carefully personalized for you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. Important: If you miss doses for 2 or more days in a row, do NOT restart your usual dose on your own — call your doctor right away. You may need to start over at a lower dose to avoid serious side effects.
storage: Store clozapine tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep the orally disintegrating tablets (ODTs) in their original packaging and use them immediately after opening. Store the oral liquid suspension at room temperature and use it within 100 days of first opening. Keep all forms of this medicine away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of unused medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about medicine take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking clozapine — it can increase drowsiness and dizziness and raise your risk of serious side effects. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires you to be fully alert until you know how this medicine affects you, as it can cause significant drowsiness. Avoid getting up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as clozapine can cause dizziness or fainting, especially at the start of treatment. Avoid becoming overheated or dehydrated — drink plenty of fluids in hot weather or during exercise. Tell your doctor before taking any other prescription or over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, or supplements, especially sedatives, sleep aids, anxiety medicines, or seizure medicines. Avoid smoking or changing your smoking habits without telling your doctor, as smoking affects how your body processes clozapine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: fever, chills, sore throat, or flu-like symptoms (these may be signs of a dangerous drop in white blood cells called agranulocytosis); chest pain, shortness of breath, or a fast or irregular heartbeat; sudden weakness, difficulty speaking, or confusion (signs of a possible stroke); severe constipation, stomach pain, or no bowel movements for several days; difficulty urinating; seizures; high fever with stiff muscles and confusion (signs of a serious condition called neuroleptic malignant syndrome); thoughts of hurting yourself or others; or unusual weight gain, excessive thirst, or frequent urination. Because clozapine can seriously lower your white blood cell count, you are required to have regular blood tests (usually weekly at first, then monthly) — do not skip these appointments.
when_it_works: Clozapine does not work overnight. Most people begin to notice some improvement in their symptoms within 1 to 4 weeks, but it may take several months of treatment to feel the full benefit. It is very important to keep taking the medicine even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults: Use with caution. Older adults, especially those with dementia, may have a higher risk of serious side effects including falls, stroke, and death. Clozapine is generally not recommended for treating behavior problems related to dementia. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Clozapine may affect a newborn baby if taken during pregnancy. Do not stop your medicine without medical guidance. Breastfeeding: Clozapine passes into breast milk and may harm a nursing baby. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children and teenagers: Safety and effectiveness in patients under 18 years old have not been fully established. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have kidney or liver disease. Always tell your doctor about all your medical conditions.
